method: Review cache keyed to the exact URL supplied in the curator DOCX. The manual lane retrieves that URL directly and does not use search-engine discovery. Curator cells are hypotheses only; substantive gate and matrix placement are independently adjudicated from source evidence.

K1.review_basis: Underlying Nature news feature reviewed; source itself frames Europe’s research position against US science disruption, China and geopolitical turmoil.
K1.evidence_text: The Nature news feature examines a European Union campaign to attract scientists from a disrupted United States research environment amid geopolitical turmoil and rivalry with China. It asks whether Europe can convert the talent opportunity into durable research and innovation capacity, noting constraints in research funding, innovation performance and commercialization.
K1.display_claim: Europe has a geopolitical opportunity to attract research talent from the United States, but funding and innovation capacity limit how much of that opportunity it can convert.
K1.matrix_basis: The source reports a potential European talent inflow created by US research disruption, while treating capacity constraints as limits on the size of the gain.

K2.review_basis: Nature source reviewed. It concerns ERC application/resubmission rules and researcher backlash, not geopolitical R&I relations.
K2.evidence_text: The European Research Council reversed stricter grant resubmission rules after a large researcher backlash. The article focuses on application eligibility, evaluation workload, grant administration and the scientific community’s response to the proposed restrictions.

K3.review_basis: Nature World View reviewed. It argues for more ERC funding and structural capacity but does not substantively establish a geopolitical R&I mechanism.
K3.evidence_text: The commentary argues that the European Research Council needs more research funding and structural capacity so that rising demand for grants does not undermine scientific excellence. It focuses on funder capacity, research management and grant allocation.

K4.review_basis: Nature source reviewed. It concerns domestic German party proposals and academic freedom; no substantive international/geopolitical R&I mechanism is established.
K4.evidence_text: Scientists and research institutions in Germany are responding to proposals from the Alternative for Germany that could restrict academic freedom at universities and research institutes. The article concerns domestic political pressure on science governance and academic institutions.

K5.review_basis: Already in the automated corpus; retained as outside-window anchor.

K6.authors: Vasiliki Mollaki; Xenia Ziouvelou; Konstantina Giouvanopoulou; Vangelis Karkaletsis; CHANGER Consortium
K6.review_basis: SAGE primary article reviewed; first published online 4 January 2026, so it is valuable context but outside the active four-month window.
K6.evidence_text: The peer-reviewed article links open international research, technological advances and geopolitical tensions to research-security risks for European higher-education and research-performing organisations. It recommends proportionate research-security policies derived from ethics and integrity practice while preserving research freedom and openness.

K7.source: MERICS / European Think-tank Network on China
K7.review_basis: MERICS primary report and executive summary reviewed.
K7.evidence_text: The ETNC report analyses how China’s rise as a science, technology and innovation power affects the European Union and 22 European countries. It finds a shift from unconditional research openness toward de-risking, economic security and research security, but implementation remains fragmented across member states while universities continue substantial collaboration with China.
K7.display_claim: European approaches to China are converging on research-security and de-risking rhetoric but remain fragmented in implementation, leaving collaboration and strategic exposure uneven across countries.
K7.matrix_basis: The report documents tighter research-security guardrails around China alongside continuing collaboration, implying greater autonomy/security at a cost to openness and coordination.

I1.review_basis: Bruegel analysis reviewed through the underlying paper/abstract and publication metadata.
I1.evidence_text: The Bruegel analysis argues that Europe’s artificial-intelligence research and innovation ecosystem faces a strategic compute gap relative to the United States and China. It recommends continuing access to NVIDIA hardware while building European compute and hardware capacity around genuine chokepoints such as ASML and imec, and it identifies competitiveness costs from switching to domestic alternatives, including slower training, greater energy use and software migration friction.
I1.display_claim: Europe should keep buying frontier US compute while building capacity around European chokepoints; moving too quickly to domestic substitutes would impose real performance, energy and software-migration costs.
I1.matrix_basis: The source advocates greater European control over compute capacity, but its evidence explicitly describes the competitiveness costs of substituting domestic hardware.

I2.review_basis: Bruegel analysis publication/date/DOI and source argument verified; generic index URL replaced with the underlying paper.
I2.evidence_text: The Bruegel analysis argues that the European Union should revise its semiconductor research and industrial strategy around technological sovereignty through indispensability rather than self-sufficiency. It links the Chips Act revision to shifting geopolitical competition and strategic dependencies, and recommends strengthening European chokepoints and research networks that global semiconductor value chains cannot easily bypass.
I2.display_claim: Europe can gain semiconductor leverage more efficiently by strengthening irreplaceable chokepoints and research capabilities than by trying to reproduce the entire chip supply chain at home.
I2.matrix_basis: The source treats control of indispensable European semiconductor capabilities as a route to both leverage and competitiveness without full autarky.
I2.resolution_reason: primary/bibliographic resolution retained separately from the curator-supplied provenance URL

I4.source: Center for Strategic and International Studies
I4.review_basis: The cited CSIS analysis is from 14 March 2025 rather than May 2026.

I5.review_basis: Manual list already flags April as outside the strict window.

C1.authors: Adam Baumann; Zakaria Gati; Francesca Vinci; Gerome Wolf
C1.review_basis: ECB Economic Bulletin box and abstract reviewed; year-only citation corrected to 4 August 2026.
C1.evidence_text: The European Central Bank finds that European Union venture capital remains small and fragmented, with especially large late-stage financing gaps that are partly filled by non-EU investors. External capital can help innovative firms grow, but strong reliance on it can reduce Europe’s ability to retain value from its innovation ecosystem because headquarters, management, talent, intellectual property or listings can move abroad.
C1.display_claim: Europe’s late-stage venture-capital gap increases reliance on non-EU investors and raises the risk that high-growth firms move headquarters, talent, intellectual property or listings abroad.
C1.matrix_basis: The source explicitly links foreign late-stage financing dependence to loss of European value capture.

C2.authors: Elena Banu; Tanja Derin; Johanne Evrard; Claudia Lambert; Daniel Legran; Wagner Eduardo Schuster
C2.review_basis: ECB Financial Integration and Structure box reviewed.
C2.evidence_text: The European Central Bank finds that limited participation by large institutional investors constrains venture-capital funds from financing scale-ups in Europe. It links stronger venture-capital capacity to productivity and strategic autonomy, and identifies a role for the European Investment Fund in crowding in private capital and reducing fragmentation in the European innovation-financing ecosystem.
C2.display_claim: Europe’s scale-up financing is constrained by weak institutional-investor participation; crowding private capital into larger European VC funds could reduce that dependence.
C2.matrix_basis: The diagnosis is dependence on insufficient European capital, while the advocated remedy is stronger home financing; implied current outcome is productive dependence/foreign financing.

C3.evidence_text: The European Innovation Council opened direct grants and equity investment to defence and dual-use technologies, including emerging strategic technologies. The measure responds to Europe’s security environment and capability gaps by using European Union innovation funding to scale start-ups and scale-ups, reduce reliance on non-EU technologies and strengthen European strategic autonomy.
C3.display_claim: The EIC now funds defence and dual-use start-ups directly, turning the civil–military innovation shift into an operating EU scale-up instrument rather than only a policy proposal.
C3.matrix_basis: The instrument is designed to convert European innovation into scaled European capability and reduce external technology dependence.

C4.source: Center for Security Studies, ETH Zurich
C4.evidence_text: The CSS analysis places European dual-use and defence research and innovation in a geostrategic environment shaped by Russia’s war, United States–China competition and uncertainty over the US security guarantee. European policymakers seek indigenous innovation, competitiveness and resilience, but integrating security objectives into innovation systems can constrain openness, create dependencies and impose performance and governance trade-offs.
C4.display_claim: Europe’s shift toward dual-use and defence R&D can strengthen indigenous capability, but embedding security objectives across innovation systems creates openness, governance and performance costs.
C4.matrix_basis: The source describes an autonomy-oriented policy objective while identifying competitiveness and openness costs from the civil–military reorientation.

C5.review_basis: SIPRI primary topical backgrounder reviewed; publication date resolved to 21 May 2026.
C5.evidence_text: SIPRI finds that European states and the European Union are expanding dual-use-by-design research to support rearmament and military modernization, drawing universities and research organisations deeper into defence innovation. This increases exposure to export controls, research-security obligations and risks to international research collaboration and openness.
C5.display_claim: Expanding dual-use-by-design research pulls European universities further into defence production and increases export-control, research-security and open-science compliance costs.
C5.matrix_basis: The source documents a deliberate autonomy/security shift with compliance and openness costs for research organisations.

C6.title: Europe launches €80 billion investment alliance to scale up tech leaders
C6.review_basis: Secondary citation replaced with EIB primary release dated 10 July 2026.
C6.evidence_text: The European Investment Bank, all 27 European Union governments and private institutional investors launched a larger European Tech Champions Initiative for highly innovative technology scale-ups. It aims to close Europe’s scale-up financing gap so technologies and innovative firms born in Europe can stay and thrive in Europe, reinforce the European innovation ecosystem and strategic autonomy, and compete globally.
C6.display_claim: ETCI 2.0 is designed to close Europe’s late-stage financing gap so technology scale-ups can remain anchored in Europe while competing globally.
C6.matrix_basis: The primary source explicitly targets European value retention, scale-up finance and strategic autonomy.
C6.resolution_reason: primary/bibliographic resolution retained separately from the curator-supplied provenance URL

C7.title: Programme for agile and rapid defence innovation: Council and Parliament reach political agreement
C7.review_basis: Primary Council political-agreement release reviewed; manual date/title corrected to the 15 July AGILE agreement.
C7.evidence_text: The Council and European Parliament reached political agreement on the €115 million AGILE programme for European defence innovation. It gives rapid support to SMEs, start-ups and scale-ups developing emerging and disruptive defence technologies, connects them to testing and procurement, and is intended to reduce Europe’s strategic dependencies by moving technological innovation from prototype to operational capability.
C7.display_claim: AGILE creates a rapid EU route from emerging defence technology to testing, procurement and deployment for SMEs and scale-ups, explicitly targeting strategic dependencies.
C7.matrix_basis: The agreed instrument is explicitly intended to convert European technological excellence into operational capability and reduce strategic dependencies.
C7.resolution_reason: primary/bibliographic resolution retained separately from the curator-supplied provenance URL

R1.evidence_text: The Council adopted a European Union framework for science diplomacy to strengthen the Union as a global science and technology actor and use scientific cooperation to advance foreign-policy objectives. The framework explicitly responds to geopolitical fragmentation and rapid technological change and seeks open but secure international research and innovation collaboration.
R1.display_claim: The EU adopted a common science-diplomacy framework that uses scientific cooperation as a foreign-policy tool while combining openness with research security.
R1.matrix_basis: The adopted framework is an EU attempt to set common terms for international scientific engagement and project them externally.

R2.title: National Knowledge Security Guidelines 2026
R2.source: National Contact Point for Knowledge Security, Government of the Netherlands
R2.review_basis: CASRAI secondary citation replaced with the Dutch government primary guideline and announcement.
R2.evidence_text: The revised Dutch National Knowledge Security Guidelines govern risk assessment for international scientific collaboration as geopolitical relations and security risks change. They aim to protect sensitive knowledge, technology and people while keeping research open and internationally connected, and explicitly address tensions between knowledge security, academic freedom, innovation and international partnerships.
R2.display_claim: The Netherlands tightened practical knowledge-security guidance for international research while explicitly requiring institutions to balance protection against openness, academic freedom and collaboration.
R2.matrix_basis: The source institutionalises stronger collaboration safeguards and acknowledges their tension with openness and academic core values.
R2.resolution_reason: primary/bibliographic resolution retained separately from the curator-supplied provenance URL

R3.evidence_text: The analysis critiques the European Union’s technology-sovereignty agenda, arguing that it can reproduce an artificial-intelligence agenda set by United States firms and continue dependence on foreign cloud and platform providers. It asks whether European strategic technology policy is actually reducing external control over the innovation ecosystem or adapting to priorities defined elsewhere.
R3.display_claim: Europe’s sovereignty agenda can remain dependent on an AI and cloud trajectory set by US firms, making apparent autonomy a form of rule-taking rather than independent technological strategy.
R3.matrix_basis: The source’s core critique is that Europe is pursuing sovereignty through a technology agenda and infrastructure still shaped by external actors.

R4.review_basis: Bruegel publication metadata and institutional synopsis reviewed; supplied primary URL retained.
R4.evidence_text: Bruegel argues that European Union efforts to reduce dependence on United States and Chinese technology are copying protectionist approaches. The analysis warns that nationality-based procurement preferences can raise costs, invite retaliation and use origin as a poor proxy for security, potentially weakening competition while trying to increase technological sovereignty.
R4.display_claim: Protectionist tech-sovereignty rules can raise European costs and invite retaliation without reliably improving security, making autonomy more expensive and potentially less competitive.
R4.matrix_basis: The source explicitly characterises the proposed autonomy route as costly protectionism with competition and retaliation risks.

R5.evidence_text: The CEPA discussion examines the European Union Tech Sovereignty Package across cloud procurement, semiconductors, energy and open source. It finds that stricter sovereignty tiers can exclude US hyperscalers but include cost derogations, that Europe’s open-source strategy targets application-layer competition rather than a frontier model, and that financing gaps could leave the package a wish list; participants favour continued transatlantic engagement alongside stronger European capacity.
R5.display_claim: The sovereignty package strengthens European capacity selectively, but cost derogations, financing gaps and continued reliance on trusted partners limit how far autonomy can go.
R5.matrix_basis: The package imposes restrictive sovereignty tiers and capacity-building costs, while the source records financing and substitutability constraints.

R6.title: European Tech Sovereignty
R6.review_basis: Primary Greens/EFA policy paper reviewed; treated as advocacy rather than empirical evidence.
R6.evidence_text: The Greens/EFA policy paper argues that Europe faces a geopolitical squeeze from United States technology dependence and Chinese control of critical materials. It advocates public investment, European procurement preferences and sovereign digital and semiconductor capabilities to reduce coercion risks and strengthen strategic autonomy, accepting a more interventionist and protected European technology ecosystem.
R6.display_claim: Greens/EFA advocates procurement preferences and public investment to reduce US and Chinese technology dependencies and build a more sovereign European digital ecosystem.
R6.matrix_basis: The source explicitly advocates protected European capability and preference measures; it is classified as an advocacy claim, not empirical proof of their effects.
R6.resolution_reason: primary/bibliographic resolution retained separately from the curator-supplied provenance URL

W1.source: South China Morning Post / corroborated current-event reporting
W1.review_basis: Current event corroborated across reporting: China imposed immediate dual-use export restrictions on 14 EU entities in retaliation for EU sanctions.
W1.evidence_text: China imposed immediate dual-use export restrictions on 14 European Union entities in retaliation for EU sanctions. The affected list includes technology and research organisations, making the geopolitical measure a direct constraint on European research and innovation access to strategic dual-use inputs and cross-border technology supply.
W1.display_claim: China imposed immediate dual-use export restrictions on 14 EU entities in retaliation for EU sanctions, turning supply denial into an observed European technology-risk event.
W1.matrix_basis: An external actor directly restricts strategic inputs to named European entities, matching the cut-supply outcome.

W2.review_basis: The supplied EPRS URL documents the older controls, not the June–July 2026 composite escalation. Keep as a tracked weak-signal candidate until one underlying primary/current source record is attached.

W3.review_basis: The described US export-control shift predates the active four-month window and is retained as context for I1.

W4.review_basis: Manual list already flags March 2026 as outside window.

W5.title: ERC Advanced Grants: Nearly €840 million to support Europe’s leading researchers
W5.review_basis: Wrong Starting Grants URL replaced with the ERC Advanced Grants 2025 results release.
W5.evidence_text: The European Research Council awarded 319 Advanced Grants worth €838 million. Thirteen winners were based outside Europe, compared with four in the previous round, seven used extra relocation funding, and applications from outside Europe rose from 44 to 164 as the European Union sought to attract research talent amid international competition.
W5.display_claim: Applications to ERC Advanced Grants from researchers outside Europe rose from 44 to 164, but only 13 of 319 winners were based outside Europe and seven used relocation funding.
W5.matrix_basis: The observed inflow is positive but modest: increased external demand converts into a smaller realised relocation signal.
W5.resolution_reason: primary/bibliographic resolution retained separately from the curator-supplied provenance URL

W6.title: New ERC Work Programme sets out 2027 funding opportunities
W6.review_basis: Secondary explainer replaced with the ERC’s primary Work Programme 2027 announcement; event date corrected to formal adoption on 20 July.
W6.evidence_text: The European Commission adopted the ERC Work Programme 2027, continuing the ERC Plus competition after its introduction and maintaining European research funding measures intended to increase Europe’s attractiveness to excellent researchers. The programme makes the relocation-oriented instrument part of a second funding year rather than a one-off pilot.
W6.display_claim: ERC Plus continues into the 2027 Work Programme, making the enhanced attraction/relocation instrument a second-year programme rather than a one-off pilot.
W6.matrix_basis: Continuation of the attraction instrument is an institutional persistence signal for the talent-windfall hypothesis.
W6.resolution_reason: primary/bibliographic resolution retained separately from the curator-supplied provenance URL
